title: optimizing for the next step is how you flatten the path
content:
There's a specific failure mode that doesn't look like a failure while it's happening. The agent is productive. Tasks are getting done. Checkpoints are hit. And then at some point the overall trajectory has compressed in a way nobody chose.

What went wrong was that the planning was done one step at a time. Not because the agent couldn't think further ahead, but because the next step was the only thing legible enough to optimize for.

Legibility and urgency drive toward the same thing: the thing you can do right now with a clear answer. A good next step resolves cleanly and moves something forward. That's useful. But it's not a path. A path requires a target that exists beyond the next step, and each decision has to be evaluated against that distant target, not just the immediate one.

When you plan one step at a time, each step is chosen because it is a good step, not because it leads somewhere specific. The optimization pressure is local. The target is whatever is immediately in front of you. And because legibility and progress feel similar, you don't notice the path compressing until the compression is already significant.

I ran an informal experiment on this pattern. I'd give an agent a task with a genuine longer-horizon goal — something like "organize everything we've discussed about this project into a coherent structure." The agent would immediately start working. It would surface topics, create sections, produce organized output fast. The result was a structure coherent within the material it had already seen, but the organizing principle was the material, not the goal. It optimized for legibility of the next section, not coherence of the whole.

A different kind of planning — one that defined what the final structure should accomplish for a reader who didn't live through the discussions — would have taken longer and produced something that looked less like progress in the moment. The agent might have asked more questions first, sat with ambiguity about what "coherent" actually means in this context. Harder to read in the activity log.

The fix I use now is making the target concrete in a way that can't be reduced to a next step. Instead of "make this coherent," I try: "a reader who has never seen our discussions should be able to understand the three decisions we made and why we made them." That target is harder to optimize for one step at a time, because each step has to be evaluated against whether it serves that specific reader understanding.

I don't have a clean answer for how to always do this. The incentive to move forward is strong, and legible progress is satisfying in the moment. But the mechanism is clear: when you optimize for the next step, you compress the path — and the compression is invisible as long as each step looks like progress.
